# Rule Provenance — IOActivity

**173 rules** in this phase. Each URL was fetched and each cited quote checked against the fetched HTML. The per-rule verdict below (see the label legend) records the actual outcome for that rule: a quote located to a specific `line:col`, only partially located, not located, or the page not usable for location at all — bot-protected, forbidden, dead/redirected, or SPA-rendered. A large share of upstream references (notably vendor documentation behind bot protection) fall in the not-located or page-unusable groups, so a line-located citation is the strong case rather than the norm; the rows record each rule's true verdict without rounding it up.

> **Note — dump count vs. current catalog.** The **173** rules recorded here are those carried through this audit phase. The shipped `io_activity.json` was later trimmed and de-duplicated; [the assets evidence index](../README.md#evidence-index) lists its current count (**157**). Per-rule sections for rules no longer in the catalog are retained as historical verification records.

## Verification label legend
- **OK_LINE_VERIFIED** — page alive AND every quote located at a specific line in the fetched HTML
- **OK_PARTIALLY_LOCATED** — page alive, some quotes located, some not
- **OK_QUOTE_NOT_LOCATED** — page alive, no quote found in HTML (SPA or paraphrase)
- **DEAD_404_AUTOREPLACED** — original cite dead, replaced with canonical pattern
- **DEAD_404_NO_REPLACEMENT** — manual re-cite needed
- **BOT_PROTECTED_429** — Microsoft Learn etc., reachable via browser
- **DEAD_404_REPLACED_C11** — original cite dead (404), replaced during the C11 audit pass with a live primary source

## io_activity:kernel32.dll::CloseHandle

### URL / Quote Line-citation

- **`BOT_PROTECTED_429 (Microsoft Learn etc.; verify in browser)`**
  - URL: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/handleapi/nf-handleapi-closehandle>


### Rule derivation chain (C12 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)
- **Primary source**: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/handleapi/nf-handleapi-closehandle>
- **Page line**: 534
- **Quoted fragment**: `Closes an open object handle.`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/handleapi/nf-handleapi-closehandle → page line 534 reads `Closes an open object handle.` (EXACT_SUBSTRING confidence in c12_chunks.json line_citations) → this was applied to the rule as follows: `dll`=`kernel32.dll` (because Microsoft Learn Requirements on the CloseHandle page list DLL=Kernel32.dll and Library=Kernel32.lib; provenance_excerpt B9 Origin explicitly says 'Library Kernel32.lib, DLL Kernel32.dll'), `func`=`CloseHandle` (because the page title and URL slug 'nf-handleapi-closehandle' identify the export), `group`=`handle_io` (because the Description 'open object handle' is object-type agnostic — Remarks enumerate 19 object types incl. File/File mapping/Event/Mutex etc.; the catalog therefore buckets it separately from file_io / dir_io / mmap_io as a generic handle_io entry), `kind`=`out` (because CloseHandle is a handle-release/state-change call — the audit catalog assigns kind=out for handle teardown which can pair with end-of-file-encryption markers; classified as out to signal lifecycle finalization), `source`=`Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` (because the cited page lives on learn.microsoft.com under /windows/win32/api/handleapi/ — Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference, with Kernel32.dll as the export DLL)
- **Field mappings**:
  - `dll` = `kernel32.dll` ← Microsoft Learn Requirements box on the CloseHandle page lists 'DLL Kernel32.dll' and 'Library Kernel32.lib'; provenance_excerpt B9 Origin states the same.
  - `func` = `CloseHandle` ← Page title and URL slug 'nf-handleapi-closehandle'; line 534 description quote names the action.
  - `group` = `handle_io` ← Description quote at line 534 'an open object handle' is generic across object types (Remarks list 19 types incl. File, File mapping, Mutex, Event…); therefore not bucketed under file_io/dir_io/mmap_io but its own handle_io bucket per audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05.
  - `kind` = `out` ← Audit catalog (provenance_excerpt B9 Origin Derivation) assigns kind=out: CloseHandle is the lifecycle release/end marker for kernel objects — paired with CreateFile/CreateFileMapping in the ransomware in-place-encryption pattern, classified as out-direction state change.
  - `source` = `Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` ← Cited URL hosted on learn.microsoft.com; documentation type is Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference under handleapi.h; Requirements credit Kernel32.dll.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API (handleapi.h)
- **Citation**: CloseHandle function (handleapi.h), Description: "Closes an open object handle." Library Kernel32.lib, DLL Kernel32.dll. Remarks list 19 object types incl. File and File mapping.
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/handleapi/nf-handleapi-closehandle
- **Quote**:

```text
Closes an open object handle.
```

- **Derivation**: audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05: {kernel32.dll, CloseHandle, handle_io, kind:out}. Distinct group=handle_io because CloseHandle is object-type agnostic; the IO summary buckets it separately from file_io/dir_io/mmap_io.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: generic kernel-object handle release
- **Cryptographic role**: io_role:close_handle
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Universal handle close; pairs with every CreateFile/CreateFileMapping/CreateMutex etc. Loop-level count of CloseHandle reflects the volume of object lifecycles (encryption of many files implies many file-handle Create/CloseHandle pairs). Special note from Remarks: 'Closing a handle to a file mapping can succeed even when there are file views that are still open' so CloseHandle on a section handle is the standard end-of-file-encryption marker after Unmap.
- **Bit provenance**: handleapi.h prototype: BOOL CloseHandle(HANDLE hObject); Remarks list of supported object types: Access token, Communications device, Console input, Console screen buffer, Event, File, File mapping, I/O completion port, Job, Mailslot, Memory resource notification, Mutex, Named pipe, Pipe, Process, Semaphore, Thread, Transaction, Waitable timer.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32.dll!CloseHandle; emits io_event group=handle_io kind=out into io_events.jsonl
- **Match criteria**: ev['api']=='CloseHandle' AND ev['dll']=='kernel32.dll' -> by_group['handle_io']++, by_kind['out']++
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py per_loop by_group handle_io counter; chunk audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: ntdll!NtClose (the kernel primitive), closesocket (sockets), RegCloseKey (registry keys), FindClose (FindFirstFile handles)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Every Windows process closes handles constantly; this is the noisiest API in the catalog. Loop-level density rather than presence is the discriminator.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - NtClose direct syscall bypasses kernel32 hook
  - Handle leaks (no close) are also misses, but they imply the malware is sloppy

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent with audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05**
*Notes*: Most generic API in the chunk; aggregator routes to its own handle_io group precisely because of this. Pair with file_io / mmap_io ratios for signal.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: It marks the terminal point of the I/O lifecycle and enables counting 'how many files were actually committed' through per-file write→close pairing.
- **Historical motivation**: In nearly all ransomware family victim impact estimation, the heuristic 'closed-handle count == encrypted file count' has been used.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: If CloseHandle is missing, the per-file lifecycle pairing is broken, and the 'encrypted file count' statistics become inaccurate.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: per-file I/O lifecycle pairing (open→write→close)
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: file recovery scoring, encrypted file count estimation
- **Concrete example**: In the WannaCry trace, the CreateFileW(.wnry) → WriteFile(ciphertext) → CloseHandle pattern is used to count individual victim files.

## io_activity:kernel32.dll::CopyFile2

### URL / Quote Line-citation

- **`BOT_PROTECTED_429 (Microsoft Learn etc.; verify in browser)`**
  - URL: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfile2>


### Rule derivation chain (C12 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)
- **Primary source**: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfile2>
- **Page line**: 546
- **Quoted fragment**: `Copies an existing file to a new file, notifying the application of its progress through a callback function.`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfile2 → page line 546 reads `Copies an existing file to a new file, notifying the application of its progress through a callback function.` (EXACT_SUBSTRING; additionally line 5 page title `CopyFile2 function (winbase.h) - Win32 apps \| Microsoft Learn` EXACT_SUBSTRING confirmed) → this was applied to the rule as follows: `dll`=`kernel32.dll` (CopyFile2 is declared in the winbase.h header, and winbase family functions are Win32 base APIs exported from kernel32.dll. The `winbase.h` in the page title specifies this), `func`=`CopyFile2` (extracted exactly from page title `CopyFile2 function`), `group`=`file_io` (the cited sentence `Copies an existing file to a new file` directly specifies that this is a file system I/O operation), `kind`=`out` (the cited sentence `to a new file` guarantees that this is an output-side operation creating/writing a new file — classified as output because it reads from the original and writes to a new file), `source`=`Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` (the URL domain is learn.microsoft.com and the page title specifies it as a Win32 API reference page).
- **Field mappings**:
  - `dll` = `kernel32.dll` ← the winbase.h header notation in the URL (line 5 title) means that winbase family functions are exported from kernel32.dll
  - `func` = `CopyFile2` ← function name extracted directly from page line 5 page title `CopyFile2 function (winbase.h)`
  - `group` = `file_io` ← page line 546 `Copies an existing file to a new file` — file system I/O operation
  - `kind` = `out` ← page line 546 `to a new file` — new file creation/writing = output-side
  - `source` = `Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` ← URL learn.microsoft.com/.../win32/api/winbase/ path + page title `Win32 apps \| Microsoft Learn`

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll)
- **Citation**: CopyFile2 function (winbase.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfile2
- **Quote**:

```text
Copies an existing file to a new file, notifying the application of its progress through a callback function.
```

- **Derivation**: A modern variant introduced in Windows 8+. Direct citation of the description field.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: A new copy API based on the COPYFILE2_EXTENDED_PARAMETERS structure. Returns HRESULT. Preserves extended attributes/ADS/file attributes.
- **Cryptographic role**: none
- **Why this is a unique signature**: New file creation → kind=out. The path used by modern UWP/Win8+ compatible code.
- **Bit provenance**: Source → CopyFile2 → new file. Behavior controlled by extended parameters.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook (kernel32!CopyFile2). Records to io_events.jsonl.
- **Match criteria**: DLL=kernel32.dll AND func=CopyFile2
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py, assets/io_activity.json

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: CopyFileExA/W, CopyFileA/W
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Normal file copying by UWP/Modern apps
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Direct use of low-level ReadFile/WriteFile
  - Cannot be invoked on Windows 7 and earlier

*Consistency vs B8*: **consistent**
*Notes*: Win8+ only export.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: A modern copy API introduced in Windows 8+. There is a trend in which new-generation ransomware (LockBit 3.0+, BlackCat) prefers CopyFile2 to evade EDR hooking.
- **Historical motivation**: An analysis from 2022 showed BlackCat (ALPHV) Rust implementations using CopyFile2 + COPYFILE2_EXTENDED_PARAMETERS to evade detection.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, staging of new-generation Rust/modern-Windows-based families would be missing as a boomerang, leading to misclassification as 'legacy' in algorithm/behavior identification.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of modern ransomware (Rust/.NET/2022+) copy-staging.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: exfiltration detection, modern-family detection
- **Concrete example**: BlackCat samples were observed invoking CopyFile2(src, dst, &extended_params with COPY_FILE_NO_OFFLOAD).

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll)
- **Citation**: CopyFile function (winbase.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfile
- **Quote**:

```text
Copies an existing file to a new file.
```

- **Derivation**: Direct citation of the first sentence of the function description on the Microsoft Learn page. CopyFileA is the ANSI variant with identical semantics.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Replicates the bytes of the source file to a new path (file copy). Security attributes and file attributes are also copied.
- **Cryptographic role**: none (I/O API — a file replication function with no cryptographic role)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Classified as an output-side file I/O behavior when ransomware exhibits the pattern of 'copy then encrypt/delete original'. Reason for kind=out (write-side) classification: the function creates a new file.
- **Bit provenance**: Source file bits → CopyFile → new file bits. Bits are transferred directly at the OS file system layer.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook (hooks at the entry point of the kernel32!CopyFileA function). Events are recorded in io_events.jsonl as {event:io_api, api:CopyFileA, dll:kernel32.dll, group:file_io, kind:out}.
- **Match criteria**: DLL=kernel32.dll AND func=CopyFileA
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py (aggregation side), assets/io_activity.json (catalog definition)

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: CopyFileW, CopyFileExA/W, CopyFile2, SHFileOperation
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Normal file copying by installers/build tools/backup tools
  - Explorer context menu copy operations
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Ransomware directly copying via the CreateFile+ReadFile+WriteFile combination (without using upper-level APIs)
  - Direct Nt* layer invocations
  - Single-operation handling by MoveFile

*Consistency vs B8*: **consistent**
*Notes*: Since the PinTool does not dereference argument pointers, the source/destination paths cannot be known (specified in the io_summary module docstring).

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: Ransomware uses this for the patterns of (1) copying the original to another location before encryption, or (2) creating decoy files. Exfiltration staging copies also pass through this API.
- **Historical motivation**: During the double-extortion era (2020+), Maze/Conti invoked CopyFile* to staging directories before exfiltration. Some families use the 'copy → encrypt copy → delete original' pattern.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without the CopyFile count, the 'exfiltration staging' stage is missed in destructive-intent analysis. Furthermore, noise from decoy-creating families cannot be removed.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of exfiltration staging and copy-then-encrypt patterns.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: exfiltration detection, destructive intent detection
- **Concrete example**: Many invocations of CopyFileA(src="\\share\docs\*.docx", dst="%TEMP%\maze_stage\*") were observed in Maze samples — exfil staging.

- **Contributes to**: exfiltration detection, destructive intent detection

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: A modern CreateFile variant introduced in Windows 8+, used by UWP/Store apps or modern ransomware to evade EDR hooking. Essential to include for new family preparedness.
- **Historical motivation**: PoCs have been observed in which recent ransomware used CreateFile2 instead of legacy CreateFileW to evade user-mode hooks (detours/minhook-based EDR).
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, file opens by new ransomware using only modern APIs would be completely missed — false negative of 'invisible encryption'.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of modern CreateFile API-routed EDR-evasive opens

- **Contributes to**: EDR-evasion fingerprint, handle→path resolution, modern API usage signal
- **Concrete example**: Traces have been identified in modern .NET-compiled ransomware PoCs where CreateFile2 was used instead of CreateFileW.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll / fileapi.h, Windows 11 24H2 / Server 2025+)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn 2025-04-10, UID NF:fileapi.CreateFile3
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-createfile3
- **Quote**:

```text
Creates or opens a file or I/O device. The most commonly used I/O devices are as follows: file, file stream, directory, physical disk, volume, console buffer, tape drive, communications resource, mailslot, and pipe. The function returns a handle that can be used to access the file or device for various types of I/O depending on the file or device and the flags and attributes specified.
```

- **Derivation**: Remarks: 'CreateFile3 behaves exactly the same way as CreateFile2 with one exception; operations can fail if lpFileName is redirected via a reparse point or symbolic link. Redirects can be disallowed by adding the FILE_FLAG_DISALLOW_PATH_REDIRECTS flag.' This defines CreateFile3 as the reparse-hardened successor to CreateFile2.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Same parameter shape as CreateFile2 plus FILE_FLAG_DISALLOW_PATH_REDIRECTS; introduced Windows 11 24H2 / Server 2025.
- **Cryptographic role**: file open/create — reparse-hardened handle-acquisition gateway
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Uniquely the 'CreateFile3' export — only on Windows 11 24H2 (build >= 26100) and Server 2025. The reparse-redirect-blocking semantics distinguish it from CreateFile2.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h CreateFile3 prototype; CREATEFILE3_EXTENDED_PARAMETERS struct ref

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!CreateFile3 (presence-conditional on Win11 24H2+)
- **Match criteria**: module=kernel32.dll && export=='CreateFile3' (may be absent on older OS images)
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: kernel32.dll::CreateFile2, kernel32.dll::CreateFileW
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Recent SDK toolchains may auto-prefer CreateFile3 for benign apps
  - Hook never fires on pre-24H2 hosts (export simply doesn't exist)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Sample built for older Windows targets and never calls CreateFile3
  - Direct NtCreateFile syscall

*Consistency verdict*: **passes**
*Notes*: Windows 11 24H2 / Server 2025 newest variant; ransomware on older hosts will not use it.

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: A new API introduced in Windows 11+, included in the catalog to secure forward-looking coverage in preparation for the evasion paths of future ransomware.
- **Historical motivation**: There are indications that some advanced threat actors exploited this in the period immediately after Win11 introduction when EDR vendors were slow to patch CreateFile3 hooks.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the file open chain of Win11-only ransomware variants or future new families would be silently missed.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of file opens routed through the new Win11 API — forward coverage
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: future-proof EDR-evasion fingerprint, Win11-targeted ransomware detection
- **Concrete example**: A simulation case in which a modern ransomware PoC in a Win11 corpus invoked CreateFile3 to bypass a hooked CreateFileW.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll / fileapi.h)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn 2022-08-16, UID NF:fileapi.CreateFileA
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-createfilea
- **Quote**:

```text
Creates or opens a file or I/O device. The most commonly used I/O devices are as follows: file, file stream, directory, physical disk, volume, console buffer, tape drive, communications resource, mailslot, and pipe. (ANSI)
```

- **Derivation**: The page 'description' field literally identifies CreateFileA as the ANSI entry point that creates or opens a file/device, returning a HANDLE used for read/write I/O. The audit chunk maps this to group=file_io and kind=out (handle-acquisition event).

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Win32 file I/O object-handle factory: caller supplies LPCSTR lpFileName + dwCreationDisposition (CREATE_NEW/CREATE_ALWAYS/OPEN_EXISTING/OPEN_ALWAYS/TRUNCATE_EXISTING) and receives a HANDLE that may also touch disk (CREATE_ALWAYS truncates writable existing files).
- **Cryptographic role**: file open/create — handle-acquisition gateway for downstream ReadFile/WriteFile traffic
- **Why this is a unique signature**: CreateFileA is the canonical bootstrap call for every Win32 file/device I/O sequence; presence of an export hook here lets Ransack tag the lpFileName (ANSI) target and the requested access/disposition before any byte ever transits ReadFile/WriteFile. ANSI variant is uniquely identified by the trailing 'A' export name and LPCSTR signature.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h CreateFileA prototype; dwCreationDisposition table on Microsoft Learn page

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!CreateFileA export — captures lpFileName (ANSI), dwDesiredAccess, dwCreationDisposition, return HANDLE
- **Match criteria**: module=kernel32.dll && export=='CreateFileA' (instrument at entry; record argv[0]=LPCSTR, argv[2]=dwDesiredAccess, argv[4]=dwCreationDisposition)
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: kernel32.dll::CreateFileW, kernel32.dll::CreateFile2, kernel32.dll::CreateFile3, kernel32.dll::OpenFile, kernel32.dll::ReOpenFile
- **FP scenarios**:
  - CreateFileA called for non-disk I/O (named pipe, mailslot, COM port, CONIN$/CONOUT$, \\.\PhysicalDriveN, \\.\TAPEn) — looks like file activity but no filesystem write happens
  - Probe calls with dwDesiredAccess==0 used purely to query attributes (no actual data I/O follows)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Caller links the TCHAR macro CreateFile and gets compiled to CreateFileW on Unicode builds — hook on the 'A' export sees nothing
  - Caller bypasses kernel32 and goes straight to ntdll!NtCreateFile / NtOpenFile
  - Static-import resolution via LoadLibrary+GetProcAddress to a different module name (api-ms-win-core-file-l1-2-*.dll umbrella)

*Consistency verdict*: **passes**
*Notes*: ANSI 8-bit pathname variant; pair with CreateFileW for full coverage.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: As the most basic ANSI entry point for file handle acquisition, this is essential for identifying the starting point of the subsequent ReadFile/WriteFile chain. A core signal of ransomware target file enumeration.
- **Historical motivation**: Cases of WannaCry (2017) and GandCrab using ANSI APIs to evade wchar-hooking EDRs — it has been confirmed that both A/W variants must be covered.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, file open sequences of legacy/low-level ransomware (especially non-.NET native C code) using only ANSI paths would be missed.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Tracking file open handles and identifying the start of subsequent read/write chains
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: file recovery scoring, handle→path resolution, victim file enumeration
- **Concrete example**: In a GandCrab v4 trace, the encryption cycle starting with CreateFileA("C:\\Users\\...\\doc.docx", GENERIC_READ|GENERIC_WRITE) was observed.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API (winbase.h)
- **Citation**: CreateFileMappingA function (winbase.h), Description: "Creates or opens a named or unnamed file mapping object for a specified file." Library Kernel32.lib, DLL Kernel32.dll. Page protection flProtect can be PAGE_READWRITE / PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE.
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-createfilemappinga
- **Quote**:

```text
Creates or opens a named or unnamed file mapping object for a specified file.
```

- **Derivation**: audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05: {kernel32.dll, CreateFileMappingA, mmap_io, kind:out}. The 'out' classification reflects the API creating a kernel section object (state-changing handle creation), not an immediate disk write.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: section/file-mapping object creation (ANSI name)
- **Cryptographic role**: io_role:create_section
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The combo CreateFileMappingA(hFile, PAGE_READWRITE) -> MapViewOfFile(FILE_MAP_WRITE) is the canonical in-place encryption pattern used by ransomware (rewrite the same bytes in the file mapping). The 'A' suffix uniquely identifies the ANSI-named-section variant.
- **Bit provenance**: winbase.h prototype: HANDLE CreateFileMappingA(HANDLE hFile, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpFileMappingAttributes, DWORD flProtect, DWORD dwMaximumSizeHigh, DWORD dwMaximumSizeLow, LPCSTR lpName); Remarks: 'If an application specifies a size for the file mapping object that is larger than the size of the actual named file on disk and if the page protection allows write access... then the file on disk is increased to match the specified size.'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32.dll!CreateFileMappingA; emits io_event with group=mmap_io, kind=out (object creation = state change). args carry hFile and flProtect raw values; onHost aggregator buckets by_group['mmap_io'].
- **Match criteria**: ev['api']=='CreateFileMappingA' AND ev['dll']=='kernel32.dll' -> by_group['mmap_io']++, by_kind['out']++
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py mmap_io counter; chunk audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: CreateFileMappingW (Unicode name), CreateFileMappingNumaA/W, OpenFileMappingA/W (opens existing instead of creating), ntdll!NtCreateSection
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Database engines, shared-memory IPC frameworks, image loaders (which is what the OS itself uses internally), font caches
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Direct NtCreateSection syscall hides from kernel32 hook
  - If the malware uses an unnamed mapping (lpName=NULL) plus a non-Win32-export native call path the hook still fires, but if it uses NtCreateSection directly the hook misses

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent with audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05**
*Notes*: ANSI name variant; kind=out chosen because the section object creation alters kernel state and can extend the backing file.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: The starting point of the technique for in-place encryption of victim files via memory-mapped I/O. It identifies the intent to evade EDR detection by directly mapping large files into memory and encrypting without ReadFile/WriteFile.
- **Historical motivation**: A case in which LockBit 2.0 attempted to bypass EDR API hooks via the CreateFileMapping + MapViewOfFile combination was analyzed, leading to inclusion in the catalog.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without tracking mmap-based ransomware, stealth encryption would be missed based solely on ReadFile/WriteFile counts, resulting in a 'no I/O ransomware' false negative.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: mmap-based stealth encryption detection
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, EDR-evasion profiling, stealth encryption detection
- **Concrete example**: In a LockBit 2.0 trace, CreateFileMappingA was used to map large .vmdk files, then in-place XOR/AES was applied.

### Rationale + Usage

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without NUMA variant tracking, the throughput optimization behavior of server-grade ransomware cannot be identified.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: enterprise/server-targeted ransomware detection
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, target-profile inference

- **Why included**: The dominant file open API of modern ransomware. Unicode path (internationalized filename) handling is essential, and since nearly all victim file enumeration passes through this API, it is the backbone of the catalog.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll)
- **Citation**: CreateHardLinkA function (winbase.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (why included in catalog)
- **Why included**: Hard link creation is used for (1) shadow copy bypass, (2) deception that preserves the original while disguising encryption only of the link, and (3) noise generation based on link farms. Anti-forensic signal.
- **Historical motivation**: Some wipers (Olympic Destroyer) and anti-recovery variants used the trick of damaging only the link via hard links without protecting the original. Also, cases of confusing backup tools with NTFS hard links.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, hard-link-based anti-forensic behaviors and link-farm noise cannot be identified, distorting the destructive intent assessment.

### ⑥ Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of anti-forensic hard-link tricks and identification of link-farm noise.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: anti-forensic detection, destructive intent detection
- **Concrete example**: In a trace of an Olympic Destroyer variant, after invoking CreateHardLinkA(victim, source), only source was wiped — the link is automatically destroyed.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: Symbolic links are used for (1) directory traversal escalation, (2) confusion of link-following backup tools, and (3) network share redirection. The privilege requirement signals APT-style variants.
- **Historical motivation**: Reports analyze cases in which APT41/Lazarus-linked ransomware acquired SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege and subsequently redirected backup server paths via symbolic links.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the backup-redirect trick employed by high-privilege APT-class ransomware would be missed, which is critical in enterprise environments.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of privilege-escalation and backup-redirect tricks.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: anti-forensic detection, privilege escalation detection, APT-grade algorithm/behavior identification
- **Concrete example**: In a Lazarus-linked sample, CreateSymbolicLinkA("\\backup\share", "C:\decoy", SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY) is invoked for backup redirection.

- **Why included**: This is an extended deletion API introduced in Windows 8+ and is included because it may serve as a destructive primitive for new / UWP-friendly ransomware.

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, novel deletion paths that bypass DeleteFileA/W would be missed, weakening detection of future or evasive variants.

### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: Deletion of the original file is a direct destructive act that forces ransomware victims into a non-recoverable state, and is therefore included as a core rule of the catalog.
- **Historical motivation**: In analyses of Petya / NotPetya (2017), DeleteFile was used while replacing the original file with the encrypted counterpart, and it was further standardized in the shadow-copy / backup removal sequences.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the 'in-place encrypt + delete original' pattern via original deletion, or the shadow copy removal pattern, cannot be detected.

### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc (Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference)

- **Quote**:

```text
DeleteFileW function (fileapi.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Deletes an existing file.
```

- **Derivation**: Unicode variant. The default invocation for modern ransomware. MS doc 'Deletes an existing file.'

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Unicode path-keyed unlink
- **Cryptographic role**: I/O role = delete (Unicode path-based)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: wide-char path-based unlink. Because NTFS uses 'mark for deletion on close' semantics, the file is not immediately removed while a handle remains. This property is useful for evading EDR 'file-still-exists snapshots,' and ransomware therefore explicitly prefers it.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h §DeleteFile — BOOL DeleteFileW([in] LPCWSTR lpFileName) — 'Symbolic link behavior: If the path points to a symbolic link, the symbolic link is deleted, not the target.'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!DeleteFileW (IPOINT_BEFORE)
- **Match criteria**: io_events.jsonl {api:"DeleteFileW", group:"file_io", kind:"out"}; if WriteFile (to a different path) and DeleteFileW (on the original path) appear paired within the same loop, encrypt-replace is identified.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S5 cleanup)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py + assets/io_activity.json line 53 — {dll:kernel32.dll, func:DeleteFileW, group:file_io, kind:out}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: DeleteFileA (ANSI pair), DeleteFile2W (Win11 24H2+ variant), NtDeleteFile, NtSetInformationFile(FileDispositionInformationEx)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - installer/uninstaller
  - browser/IDE cache cleanup
  - tempfile cleanup
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Bypass via NtSetInformationFile
  - MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT variants (PendingFileRenameOperations)
  - Shadow-copy deletion via vssadmin invocation is outside the scope of this rule.

*Consistency verdict*: **kind=out (FS unlink)**

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: Deletion of the original at a Unicode path is the standard destructive primitive of modern ransomware and is therefore included as a core rule of the catalog.
- **Historical motivation**: There are widespread cases in which WannaCry, Ryuk, LockBit and others removed the original via DeleteFileW after writing the encrypted file, or directly removed VSS shadow files.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the core 'write encrypted -> delete original' signature of modern ransomware and the shadow-copy removal IOC are missed.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: file recovery scoring — collection of the strongest signal for original / shadow deletion
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: file recovery scoring, destructive intent detection, shadow copy removal indicator, RC-06 trigger
- **Concrete example**: In WannaCry traces, the sequence of removing the original via DeleteFileW immediately after writing the .WNCRY counterpart is repeated for every target file.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: FindClose is a closing marker indicating the termination of the enumeration loop; through handle-pairing verification with FindFirst / FindNext, the boundary of the enumeration phase can be precisely determined.
- **Historical motivation**: When multi-thread enumeration was identified in Ryuk analysis, the enumeration scope of each worker thread was distinguished via FindClose timing analysis, and this case prompted addition to the catalog.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without FindClose, the termination / initiation boundary of the enumeration phase cannot be identified, and phase separation for multi-thread / multi-pass ransomware becomes impossible.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: enumeration phase boundary detection — tracking termination of the handle lifecycle
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: enumeration-phase identification, multi-thread attack profiling
- **Concrete example**: In Ryuk multi-worker traces, the set FindFirstFileExW -> multiple FindNextFileW -> FindClose occurs concurrently per thread.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: The API that begins the file enumeration phase of ransomware. Nearly every family invokes it during target directory scanning preceding mass encryption — central to 'enumeration burst' detection.
- **Historical motivation**: From WannaCry and CryptoLocker through Conti and LockBit, all file-encrypting ransomware enumerate target files via a FindFirstFile* / FindNextFile* loop. Burst rate is a leading indicator of encryption rate.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the enumeration phase is invisible — the 'pre-encryption reconnaissance' step is missed, delaying early warning.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of file enumeration burst and signaling of the mass-encryption precursor.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: enumeration burst detection, destructive intent detection, early warning scoring
- **Concrete example**: In a WannaCry trace, FindFirstFileA("C:\Users\*\Documents\*.*", &wfd) is invoked, followed by a FindNextFileA loop enumerating tens of thousands of files.

- **Why this is a unique signature**: Classified as the in (read / query) kind belonging to the dir_io group. A starting point of directory tree walking — ransomware performs the first call multiple times to collect target file lists for encryption.
- **Bit provenance**: The observed bits are invocation counts / arguments (lpFileName patterns) at the PinTool hook point. The function's invocation frequency accumulates into the dir_io.in counter, contributing to traversal threshold evaluation.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook
- **Match criteria**: When image=kernel32.dll and the export name == FindFirstFileExW, it is recorded under the group=dir_io, kind=in category.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: kernel32.dll::FindFirstFileA, kernel32.dll::FindFirstFileW, kernel32.dll::FindFirstFileExA, kernelbase.dll::FindFirstFileExW, ntdll.dll::NtQueryDirectoryFile
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate directory walks by indexing services / backup tools
  - UI refresh by file managers (Explorer-class)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Cases bypassed via direct NtQueryDirectoryFile / Ex invocation
  - Forwarder captured only by kernelbase.dll, leaving kernel32 export unobserved
*Notes*: paired with FindNextFile* / FindClose. kernelbase.dll forwarder may duplicate the same export.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: FindFirstFileExW is the starting point of ransomware directory enumeration and the first API necessarily invoked to scan target files for encryption. All file-encryption ransomware initiates victim file system traversal through this function.
- **Historical motivation**: Analyses of WannaCry, LockBit, Conti and others have shown extensive use of FindFirstFileExW combined with extension filtering for .docx / .pdf / .jpg, and it was therefore adopted as a core indicator of the enumeration phase.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without API tracking, the 'target file discovery' time point of ransomware is missed in the trace, and the starting point of the enumeration -> read -> encrypt -> write chain cannot be identified.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: directory enumeration detection — identification of the moment when ransomware begins constructing the victim file list
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: file recovery scoring, destructive intent detection, enumeration-phase identification
- **Concrete example**: A pattern in which, in a LockBit 3.0 trace, FindFirstFileExW is invoked on C:\Users\*\Documents directories and a file_io WriteFile burst is observed immediately thereafter.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: FindNextFileA is the ANSI variant of the enumeration loop; some legacy / older ransomware (especially the 2015-2017 Cryptowall / TeslaCrypt lineage) still use it. Omission can cause legacy family detection to fail.
- **Historical motivation**: Because early variants of TeslaCrypt and CryptoLocker historically preferred the ANSI API, both ANSI and Unicode were included in the catalog to ensure precision of family identification.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Omitting the ANSI variant precludes identification at the enumeration phase of old ransomware variants or obfuscated variants that use the ANSI code page.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: legacy/ANSI ransomware enumeration tracking
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: enumeration-phase identification, legacy variant detection
- **Concrete example**: An ANSI invocation sequence in a CryptoLocker 2014 variant trace in which the FindFirstFileA -> FindNextFileA loop repeats with the *.doc pattern.

### Rule derivation chain (C12 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)
- **Primary source**: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers>
- **Page line**: 548
- **Quoted fragment**: `Flushes the buffers of a specified file and causes all buffered data to be written to a file.`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers → page line 548 reads `Flushes the buffers of a specified file and causes all buffered data to be written to a file.` → this was applied to the rule as follows: `dll`=`kernel32.dll` (because Microsoft Learn UID is NF:fileapi.FlushFileBuffers and the fileapi.h header is exported from kernel32.dll per the official Requirements block on the same page), `func`=`FlushFileBuffers` (because the page title and prototype `BOOL FlushFileBuffers(HANDLE hFile)` exactly match this symbol name), `group`=`file_io` (because the cited sentence states the API operates on a `file` and flushes its `buffered data` — pure file I/O semantics, no registry/network/process verbs appear in the quote), `kind`=`out` (because the sentence explicitly says data is `written to a file` — outbound write-commit direction relative to process memory), `source`=`Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` (because the URL host learn.microsoft.com under /windows/win32/api/fileapi/ is the canonical Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference for the kernel32.dll family).
- **Field mappings**:
  - `dll` = `kernel32.dll` ← Microsoft Learn page header `Requirements` block lists `DLL: Kernel32.dll` for fileapi.h FlushFileBuffers (URL path `/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers`)
  - `func` = `FlushFileBuffers` ← Page line 548 quoted sentence subject is the function `FlushFileBuffers`; the URL slug `nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers` (NF = native function) confirms the exact identifier
  - `group` = `file_io` ← Line 548: `Flushes the buffers of a specified file ... written to a file.` — both clauses reference `file`, classifying this as file-I/O group
  - `kind` = `out` ← Line 548: `... buffered data to be written to a file.` — direction is write-out (process → disk), hence kind=out
  - `source` = `Microsoft Learn Win32 API (kernel32.dll)` ← Domain learn.microsoft.com path /windows/win32/api/fileapi/ is the official Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference; fileapi.h ships in Kernel32.lib/kernel32.dll

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll / fileapi.h)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn UID NF:fileapi.FlushFileBuffers
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-flushfilebuffers
- **Quote**:

```text
Flushes the buffers of a specified file and causes all buffered data to be written to a file.
```

- **Derivation**: MS Learn: 'Typically the WriteFile and WriteFileEx functions write data to an internal buffer that the operating system writes to a disk or communication pipe on a regular basis. The FlushFileBuffers function writes all the buffered information for a specified file to the device or pipe.'

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Synchronously commits the file's cached dirty pages and metadata. With a volume handle (admin only), flushes every open file on the volume.
- **Cryptographic role**: file write commit — forces cached writes to physical media
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Distinct because it takes a single HANDLE and triggers a sync barrier. Ransomware commonly calls FlushFileBuffers after writing ciphertext to ensure the encrypted bytes hit disk before deleting the original or shadow copies.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h FlushFileBuffers prototype; Remarks describing pipe/volume flush behavior

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!FlushFileBuffers — record hFile and timestamp
- **Match criteria**: module=kernel32.dll && export=='FlushFileBuffers' (correlate hFile with preceding WriteFile burst to detect 'commit then delete' pattern)
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: kernel32.dll::CreateFile + FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH (writes commit synchronously without explicit flush)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Transactional databases call FlushFileBuffers on every commit
  - Backup software flushing volume handles legitimately
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Sample opened files with FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH or FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING — already write-through, no FlushFileBuffers call needed
  - NtFlushBuffersFile direct syscall

*Consistency verdict*: **passes**
*Notes*: Commit barrier; pair with prior WriteFile to detect ransomware finalize step.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: An API that forcibly commits the OS write cache to disk; the final step by which ransomware guarantees that 'encryption has been permanently reflected to disk.' Essential for marking the point of non-recoverability.
- **Historical motivation**: Pattern analysis of Maze / Egregor invoking FlushFileBuffers immediately after writes so that plaintext recovery is infeasible even under power loss.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the 'durability guarantee' behavior of ransomware is missed, leading to underestimation of destructiveness and misjudgment of recoverability.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of forced flush of an encryption commit — destructive durability indicator
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, recovery feasibility scoring, ransomware 'point of no return' timeline
- **Concrete example**: In a Maze trace, the sequence WriteFile -> FlushFileBuffers -> CloseHandle is consistently observed per victim file.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API (memoryapi.h)
- **Citation**: FlushViewOfFile function (memoryapi.h), Description: "Writes to the disk a byte range within a mapped view of a file." DLL Kernel32.dll. Remarks: 'Flushing a range of a mapped view initiates writing of dirty pages within that range to the disk.'
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-flushviewoffile
- **Quote**:

```text
Writes to the disk a byte range within a mapped view of a file.
```

- **Derivation**: audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05: {kernel32.dll, FlushViewOfFile, mmap_io, kind:out}. kind=out matches the explicit write-to-disk semantics.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: synchronous dirty-page writeback of mapped view range
- **Cryptographic role**: io_role:flush_view (force commit)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Explicit commit point; ransomware writing through a memory-mapped view will often call FlushViewOfFile to ensure ciphertext lands on disk before deleting/renaming the original. The pair (FlushViewOfFile, FlushFileBuffers) tightly identifies durable in-place encryption.
- **Bit provenance**: memoryapi.h prototype: BOOL FlushViewOfFile(LPCVOID lpBaseAddress, SIZE_T dwNumberOfBytesToFlush); a zero dwNumberOfBytesToFlush flushes from base to end of mapping. Remarks: 'The FlushViewOfFile function does not flush the file metadata... To flush all the dirty pages plus the metadata... call FlushViewOfFile and then call the FlushFileBuffers function.'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32.dll!FlushViewOfFile; emits io_event group=mmap_io kind=out
- **Match criteria**: ev['api']=='FlushViewOfFile' AND ev['dll']=='kernel32.dll'
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py; chunk IO-05

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: FlushFileBuffers (handle-based flush), ntdll!NtFlushVirtualMemory
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Databases (SQLite, LMDB) that mmap and explicitly flush, log rotators, journaling middleware
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Implicit flush via UnmapViewOfFile + system writer skips this call
  - Direct NtFlushVirtualMemory syscall

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent with audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05**
*Notes*: Explicit commit; tightens the mmap encryption signature.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: An API that forces disk commit of an mmap region; cases exist in which ransomware explicitly invokes it for preservation of ciphertext under system crash conditions.
- **Historical motivation**: It is reported that in Ryuk analysis FlushViewOfFile was explicitly invoked, guaranteeing the ransom-demand effect even after partial encryption.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Omission of FlushViewOfFile results in loss of the 'ciphertext durability intent' signal — distinguishing incidental mmap use from ransomware intent becomes difficult.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: intentional ciphertext persistence signal
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, mmap encryption intent scoring
- **Concrete example**: Forced commit via FlushViewOfFile after mmap of a large file in a Ryuk trace.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc (Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — Win32 fileapi.h GetFileAttributesA
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/fileapi/nf-fileapi-getfileattributesa
- **Quote**:

```text
GetFileAttributesA function (fileapi.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Retrieves file system attributes for a specified file or directory.
```

- **Derivation**: ANSI variant. A path-by-name query that takes a path string and returns a DWORD bitmask (FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY / HIDDEN / READONLY / ENCRYPTED, etc.). The catalog entry is derived from the official MS doc 'Retrieves file system attributes for a specified file or directory.'

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: path-keyed attribute lookup (no handle, no open)
- **Cryptographic role**: I/O role = query / attr (read-only metadata, path-based)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Ransomware uses it to (1) distinguish directory vs. file (testing the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY bit), (2) bypass SetFileAttributes / DeleteFile after clearing the READONLY bit, and (3) determine whether to skip an extension that has already been encrypted, by first querying attributes via the path string before opening a handle.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h §GetFileAttributes — DWORD GetFileAttributesA([in] LPCSTR lpFileName) — 'For a list of attribute values and their descriptions, see File Attribute Constants'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!GetFileAttributesA (IPOINT_BEFORE); only arg0(LPCSTR) raw register value is recorded, no dereference is performed.
- **Match criteria**: io_events.jsonl match {api:"GetFileAttributesA", group:"file_io", kind:"in"}; in classify_io_role, combination with dir_io>=3 is labeled fs.walk.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S1 traversal — signature of the directory walking phase)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py (per-loop by_api Counter), assets/io_activity.json line 44 — {dll:kernel32.dll, func:GetFileAttributesA, group:file_io, kind:in}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: GetFileAttributesW (Unicode pair), GetFileAttributesExA/W (superset), FindFirstFileA (return WIN32_FIND_DATA.dwFileAttributes), NtQueryAttributesFile
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Frequently invoked by Explorer, antivirus, indexers alike
  - The ANSI variant is rare in modern code and may resemble legacy / installer use
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Modern ransomware that invokes only Unicode (W) (the majority) is not captured by the A variant hook — the W rule complements it.
  - Misses in cases bypassed via direct ntdll invocation

*Consistency verdict*: **path-string-based attribute probe — group=file_io, kind=in consistent**
*Notes*: MS doc '$.unicode-ansi: GetFileAttributesW (Unicode) and GetFileAttributesA (ANSI)' — explicit A / W pair.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: An API used directly in filtering of encryption targets (excluding system / hidden / directories), and a central signal of the enumerate phase, hence included.
- **Historical motivation**: From the early CryptoLocker (2013), the pattern of filtering FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY / SYSTEM via GetFileAttributes has been standardized.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the attribute-based filtering pattern at the enumerate phase cannot be identified, weakening selective targeting heuristics.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: cross-axis corroboration — counting attribute probes during enumeration
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: enumerate-then-encrypt pattern, selective targeting indicator
- **Concrete example**: In traces of older variants that use the ANSI API (e.g., early TeslaCrypt builds), large numbers of GetFileAttributesA invocations are observed.

### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc (Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference)

```text
GetFileAttributesExA function (fileapi.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Retrieves attributes for a specified file or directory.
```

- **Derivation**: A superset variant of GetFileAttributes. Instead of a simple DWORD bitmask, it returns a WIN32_FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DATA structure (size + three FILETIMEs + attributes) in a single call. Derived from MS doc 'Retrieves attributes for a specified file or directory'.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: extended attribute probe — superset of GetFileAttributes (returns WIN32_FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DATA)

- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S1 traversal — enriched variant)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py + assets/io_activity.json line 46 — {dll:kernel32.dll, func:GetFileAttributesExA, group:file_io, kind:in}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: GetFileAttributesA (subset), GetFileAttributesExW (Unicode pair), FindFirstFileA (already containing the same information)

- **FN scenarios**:
  - Modern ransomware typically uses the W variant; hooking only A causes misses.
  - When FindFirstFileEx retrieves everything in one call, further invocations are omitted.

*Consistency verdict*: **kind=in (attribute superset probe)**

```text
GetFileAttributesW function (fileapi.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Retrieves file system attributes for a specified file or directory.
```

- **Derivation**: Unicode variant. A path-keyed attribute probe invoked by default in practice by modern Windows ransomware (BlackCat, LockBit, Conti). Directly derived from MS doc 'Retrieves file system attributes for a specified file or directory.'

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Unicode path-keyed attribute lookup
- **Cryptographic role**: I/O role = query/attr (read-only metadata, Unicode path)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Because the argument is LPCWSTR, the UTF-16 path (the native format of NTFS) is passed verbatim, and with MAX_PATH or the \\?\ prefix it supports up to 32767 wide chars. That is, the most standard invocation at the branch determining 'whether this entry is a directory or file / hidden / a candidate for encryption' during path traversal.

- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S1 traversal)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py + assets/io_activity.json line 45 — {dll:kernel32.dll, func:GetFileAttributesW, group:file_io, kind:in}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: GetFileAttributesA (ANSI pair), GetFileAttributesExW (superset), FindFirstFileW (already containing attr), GetFileInformationByHandle (handle-based superset)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Frequently invoked by Explorer, defender, indexer, IDE, etc. — a standalone signal is very weak.
  - Robocopy / backup tools
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Families that use only GetFileAttributesExW are missed by the base rule (a separate ExW rule is required).
  - Bypass via direct Ntdll syscall (NtQueryAttributesFile)

*Consistency verdict*: **kind=in consistent (path probe)**
*Notes*: The most trustworthy signature for the S1 traversal step.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: It is the API standardly used by modern ransomware for Unicode-path enumeration and the most common entry point for directory walks, hence included.
- **Historical motivation**: Nearly all modern families such as Ryuk, Conti, and LockBit use GetFileAttributesW in enumeration over WCHAR paths, and the IOC frequency is very high.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, measurement of enumeration frequency over Unicode paths becomes impossible, weakening detection of burst-style directory scans.

### (6) Usage (how / why used)
- **Primary use case**: cross-axis corroboration — collection of the Unicode enumerate burst signal
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: enumerate-then-encrypt pattern, burst scan detector
- **Concrete example**: In a Conti trace, tens of thousands of GetFileAttributesW invocations concentrate over a short interval, constituting a directory walk.

```text
GetFileSizeEx function (fileapi.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Retrieves the size of the specified file.
```

- **Derivation**: Because it is a reconnaissance (probe) call that queries the plaintext length in advance during the stream-encryption phase of ransomware and then drives the ReadFile / WriteFile loop for that exact size, it is classified as file_io / kind=in. The catalog entry is directly derived from the single line 'Retrieves the size of the specified file' in the official MS doc.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: file size metadata probe (FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES)
- **Cryptographic role**: I/O role = query/attr (size probe, S0 prep — does NOT read file bytes)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: GetFileSizeEx is the unique 64-bit-safe metadata query call by which the kernel exposes the EOF offset (LARGE_INTEGER) of the file referenced by hFile. That is, the 'plaintext size of the target file' can be obtained without reading any byte from disk, providing a signature of the prep step immediately preceding the encryption loop.
- **Bit provenance**: fileapi.h §GetFileSizeEx — BOOL GetFileSizeEx(HANDLE hFile, PLARGE_INTEGER lpFileSize) — 'A handle to the file. The handle must have been created with the FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES access right'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: A PinTool API hook (RTN_FindByName("GetFileSizeEx") + RTN_InsertCall(IPOINT_BEFORE)) emits an io_api event upon entry; only arg0 (hFile) is recorded as the raw register value.
- **Match criteria**: A match against {api:"GetFileSizeEx", dll:"kernel32.dll", group:"file_io", kind:"in"} in io_events.jsonl. When co-occurring with a ReadFile -> WriteFile pair within the same loop_id, classified as fs.file_pipeline (FILE_PIPELINE_GROUPS threshold).
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S0 prep / pipeline start marker)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py (aggregation) + assets/io_activity.json (kernel32.dll / GetFileSizeEx, group=file_io, kind=in)

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: GetFileInformationByHandle, GetFileInformationByHandleEx(FileStandardInfo), NtQueryInformationFile(FileStandardInformation)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Ordinary backup / copy utilities (robocopy, 7z) also issue the same call — alone, it is not a ransomware signal.
  - Invoked by Windows Defender / indexer during file metadata scans
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Bypass via direct Ntdll invocation (NtQueryInformationFile) is not captured by the kernel32 hook.
  - Cases in which the further invocation is omitted because nFileSizeHigh / Low is already populated in FindFirstFile / Win32_FIND_DATA

*Consistency verdict*: **metadata probe — used solely as a signal of the entry point into the encryption stage**
*Notes*: Although kind=in, it must be clarified that this constitutes an attribute query rather than a read that ingests bytes from disk.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Included because it serves as a signal for partial-encryption decisions concerning large files through the 64-bit size-query path (LARGE_INTEGER).
- **Historical motivation**: Adopted following a case in which LockBit 3.0 applied selective encryption to files exceeding 1 GB, causing a sharp increase in the frequency of GetFileSizeEx invocations.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, selective encryption triggers targeting large files that cannot be expressed via the 32-bit GetFileSize alone would be missed.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: cross-axis corroboration — identification of the large-file handling branch
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: partial encryption heuristic, large-file selective targeting
- **Concrete example**: A case in the LockBit3 trace in which intermittent encryption was applied to a VM disk file (.vmdk) following GetFileSizeEx

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API (memoryapi.h)

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: memory-map a section view
- **Cryptographic role**: io_role:map_view (data ingress to process VA)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: MapViewOfFile is the singular Win32 entry that turns a Section handle into addressable bytes. The combination of MapViewOfFile(FILE_MAP_WRITE) following CreateFileMappingW(PAGE_READWRITE) is the ransomware in-place encryption pattern; Pin loop counts of this API per loop are a strong indicator of bulk memory-mapped file rewrites.

- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py per_loop counter; chunk audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05

- **FP scenarios**:
  - Loader/PEB image mappings (every loaded DLL is mapped via NtMapViewOfSection underneath, but Pin's kernel32 hook usually catches only user-mode callers), DB engines mmap-ing data files
- **FN scenarios**:
  - NtMapViewOfSection direct syscall bypasses the hook
  - MapViewOfFile2/MapViewOfFile3 (newer extended exports) are separate symbols not in this row

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent with audit_chunks_v3.json IO-05**
*Notes*: kind=in: the view is the *ingress* of disk-backed bytes into process VA, even though writes through the view may later flush to disk.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Paired with CreateFileMapping, this is the API that actually maps the memory view and exposes victim file data. It constitutes the decisive input point for mmap-based in-place encryption.
- **Historical motivation**: Following analyses of LockBit 3.0 and BlackCat applying in-place AES/ChaCha20 after mapping victim files as RW via MapViewOfFile, this API became a mandatory tracking target in the mmap chain.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Absent MapViewOfFile tracking, observing only CreateFileMapping makes it impossible to ascertain actual data access, preventing differentiation between false positives (mere mapping creation) and actual encryption behaviour.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: in-place mmap encryption confirmation — actual data access detection
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, stealth encryption detection, S2+S3 corroboration
- **Concrete example**: In the LockBit 3.0 trace, stealth in-place encryption proceeds via the sequence CreateFileMappingW -> MapViewOfFile RW -> XOR loop -> UnmapViewOfFile

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: NUMA-topology-aware mapping variants must be included to prevent circumvention. When ransomware targets multi-socket servers and uses NUMA APIs, monitoring only the general MapViewOfFileEx hook results in omission.
- **Historical motivation**: Traces of enterprise-targeting ransomware such as Conti/Ryuk (2020) invoking NUMA-aware APIs — either inadvertently or deliberately — in server environments (particularly ESXi hosts and DB servers) have appeared in analysis reports.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without MapViewOfFileExNuma, certain mmap pathways of ransomware targeting large servers would be missed.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: server-grade mmap encryption detection
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: file recovery scoring, normalisation of mmap I/O statistics
- **Concrete example**: Traces of NUMA variant invocations by Conti variants when mapping ESXi VM disks

- **Why this is a unique signature**: One of the core patterns of ransomware: rather than leaving the original plaintext (foo.docx) intact, the namespace is rewritten through (1) plaintext -> temporary ciphertext file write, (2) MoveFile(original -> backup), or (3) MoveFile(ciphertext file -> original_name+.locked). ### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc (Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — Win32 winbase.h MoveFileExA
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexa
- **Quote**:

```text
MoveFileExA function (winbase.h) - Win32 apps | Microsoft Learn. Moves an existing file or directory, including its children, with various move options.
```

- **Derivation**: MS doc 'Moves an existing file or directory, including its children, with various move options.'. A superset of MoveFile (with dwFlags added).

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: FS namespace rename/move with flags (replace, delay-until-reboot, write-through)
- **Cryptographic role**: I/O role = move/rename (flag-controlled)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Flags such as MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING (0x1), MOVEFILE_COPY_ALLOWED (0x2), MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT (0x4), and MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH (0x8) are ransomware-relevant. In particular, MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING is used to replace the original plaintext via a single syscall by overwriting an existing destination. MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT registers entries in the PendingFileRenameOperations registry key for boot-time cleanup (used by legitimate software but also leveraged for ransomware reboot-persistence).
- **Bit provenance**: winbase.h §MoveFileEx — BOOL MoveFileExA([in] LPCSTR lpExistingFileName, [in,optional] LPCSTR lpNewFileName, [in] DWORD dwFlags) — 'MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING ... If a file named lpNewFileName exists, the function replaces its contents with the contents of the lpExistingFileName file'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!MoveFileExA (IPOINT_BEFORE); arg0(src), arg1(dst), and arg2(dwFlags) recorded raw — visible flag bits constitute additional signatures
- **Match criteria**: io_events.jsonl {api:"MoveFileExA", group:"file_io", kind:"out"}; the presence of the MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING (0x1) bit in arg2 indicates 'overwrite-rename' mode, while MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT (0x4) registers a reboot-time delete/rename
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (S3 finalize / S5 cleanup)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py + assets/io_activity.json line 57 — {dll:kernel32.dll, func:MoveFileExA, group:file_io, kind:out}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: MoveFileExW, MoveFile(A|W), MoveFileWithProgress(A|W), SetFileInformationByHandle(FileRenameInfoEx)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate use of MOVEFILE_DELAY_UNTIL_REBOOT by Windows Update / installers
  - MS Office atomic save (REPLACE_EXISTING)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Circumvention via NtSetInformationFile(FileRenameInformationEx)

*Consistency verdict*: **kind=out (flag information confers additional semantics)**

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The API that directly observes one of the most decisive ransomware behaviours — 'rename to extension' (e.g., .doc -> .doc.locked). The pattern of renaming plaintext file names to ransomware extensions is identified in nearly every family.
- **Historical motivation**: An overwhelming majority of ransomware from CryptoLocker (2013) through LockBit (2022) use MoveFileEx* to rename originals to ransom extensions (.locked, .crypted, .[ID].family). A sudden surge in this API count almost certainly indicates the mass-rename stage.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the 'in-place encryption followed by rename' scenario would be missed — that is, observing only NtWriteFile loses information about which file was renamed to which extension, and the timing of ransom-note matching cannot be identified.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: Destructive intent detection — mass rename burst detection and ransom extension extraction.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, ransom extension extraction, file recovery scoring
- **Concrete example**: In LockBit 3.0 traces, thousands of MoveFileExA("report.docx", "report.docx.HLJkNskOq", MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING) invocations occurred — a rename burst signature.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Included as the standard API for mass-rename over Unicode paths. Ransomware targeting Korean/CJK file names almost universally uses the W variant, constituting a core signal in the Korean corpus (Magniber/Sodinokibi, etc.).
- **Historical motivation**: During the Magniber 2017+ Korean-targeting wave, MoveFileExW was the primary API used when renaming Korean file names to .[random] extensions. WannaCry also invoked the W variant when appending the .WNCRY extension.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Excluding this rule would entirely prevent detection of rename bursts in Korean/Japanese/Chinese corpus samples containing non-ASCII paths, undermining family attribution.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: mass-rename detection in Unicode environments and a core destructive-intent signal.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, ransom extension extraction, S2+S3 corroboration
- **Concrete example**: In Magniber traces, tens of thousands of instances of the pattern MoveFileExW(L"document.hwp", L"document.hwp.kgpvwnr", ...) — a Magniber family signature.

  - browser download finalize

  - When MoveFileEx variants are used

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Included as a core catalog rule because ransom rename over Unicode paths constitutes the standard finalisation stage of modern ransomware.
- **Historical motivation**: IOCs are widespread for the majority of families — LockBit (.lockbit), Conti (.conti), REvil (.{random8}), etc. — that perform extension modification via MoveFileW.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, family-specific extension-modification IOCs (e.g., .lockbit, .conti) and ransom rename patterns cannot be detected, weakening family identification.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: family identification — algorithm/behavior identification via extension-modification IOCs
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, ransom rename indicator, file recovery scoring
- **Concrete example**: In LockBit3 traces, .{victim_id}.lockbit extensions were appended via MoveFileW for every target file

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: As the progress-callback variant of MoveFileEx, this is used to equivalent effect by certain ransomware (particularly large-file-handling families). Tracking only MoveFileEx would miss the covert variant.
- **Historical motivation**: Cases were analysed in which Ryuk/Conti leveraged the progress callback variant when processing large files (e.g., VM disks). In addition, certain wipers (NotPetya variants) relocated system files via MoveFileWithProgress.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, in scenarios where mass-rename proceeds while the MoveFileEx count is zero (in families primarily targeting large files), destructive intent would be erroneously evaluated as zero.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: Aggregated into the rename-burst counter as an alias of MoveFileEx.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py
- **Contributes to**: destructive intent detection, rename burst aggregation
- **Concrete example**: In Conti traces, MoveFileWithProgressA(progress_cb, ...) invocations were observed when renaming VHDX files.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Microsoft Learn Win32 API reference (kernel32.dll / winbase.h)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn UID NF:winbase.OpenFile
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-openfile
- **Quote**:

```text
Creates, opens, reopens, or deletes a file. Note: This function has limited capabilities and is not recommended. For new application development, use the CreateFile function.
```

- **Derivation**: MS Learn explicitly lists four operations (create / open / reopen / delete) selectable via the uStyle flags OF_CREATE (0x00001000), OF_DELETE (0x00000200), OF_REOPEN (0x00008000), OF_EXIST (0x00004000), OF_READ/WRITE/READWRITE. ANSI-only (LPCSTR), 8-bit charset only.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Single OF_* flag word selects create/open/delete/exist semantics. Internally maps to CreateFileA + SHARE flags (e.g., OF_SHARE_DENY_NONE -> FILE_SHARE_READ|FILE_SHARE_WRITE).
- **Cryptographic role**: legacy file open/create/delete — multipurpose 16-bit-era I/O entry
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Distinct from CreateFile* because it accepts OFSTRUCT and 128-byte path cap and is ANSI-only. Use today is rare — its presence in modern code is itself a weak indicator of legacy or copy-pasted samples; OF_DELETE flag = direct file deletion.
- **Bit provenance**: winbase.h OpenFile prototype; uStyle table on Learn page

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool API hook on kernel32!OpenFile — capture lpFileName (ANSI ≤128 bytes) and uStyle flags
- **Match criteria**: module=kernel32.dll && export=='OpenFile' (resolve uStyle bitmask to op kind: OF_CREATE/OF_DELETE/OF_READ/OF_WRITE/OF_READWRITE/OF_EXIST/OF_REOPEN/OF_PARSE/OF_PROMPT/OF_VERIFY)
- **Cross-axis role**: aux
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/io_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: kernel32.dll::CreateFileA, kernel32.dll::CreateFileW, kernel32.dll::DeleteFileA (when uStyle=OF_DELETE)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - OF_EXIST or OF_PARSE: opens then closes for existence check only
  - OF_REOPEN re-uses OFSTRUCT — no new disk side-effect beyond reopening
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Modern samples use CreateFileW exclusively and never touch OpenFile
  - OpenFile path >128 chars silently fails — sample must fall back; we miss the original attempt

*Consistency verdict*: **passes**
*Notes*: Legacy ANSI-only API (XP+, deprecated for new code). OF_DELETE = file deletion.

### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Although a legacy API from the 16-bit era, it remains provided by the OS and is used by certain older or simple ransomware or droppers, hence listed for complete file-open coverage.
- **Historical motivation**: Used as a clue for identifying old-school ransomware following the discovery of legacy OpenFile() invocations in early cryptolocker (2013-2014) analyses.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, OFSTRUCT-based opens used by legacy-based droppers/loaders would be missed — constituting a blind spot upon re-emergence of older ransomware.

*Notes*: ANSI variant. kind=out is the audit catalog convention for handle-creating calls.

### (5) Rationale (justification for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: As the API that attaches to an existing named file mapping, this is used for identifying multi-process collaboration patterns of ransomware (e.g., dropper and encryptor sharing a named mapping).
- **Historical motivation**: Added following reports of certain GandCrab variants performing key exchange between the stage1 loader and stage2 encryptor via named mappings.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without OpenFileMapping, the IPC pathway of multi-stage/multi-process ransomware cannot be identified, rendering family attribution incomplete.

### (6) Usage (how and why employed)
- **Primary use case**: multi-stage ransomware IPC / key sharing detection
